title: Verifier‑Assisted versus One‑Shot LLM Intent→Configuration: A Paired NetOpsTraceBench Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed NetOpsTraceBench, a paired comparison of a one‑shot LLM intent→configuration pipeline and a verifier‑assisted generate–validate–repair pipeline on 1,200 intent→config episodes (1,199 complete pairs). Using requested_model = gpt-5-mini, a deterministic NetOps validator, and Mininet‑style emulation, we applied a preregistered binary episode success rule (validator accepts final config AND emulator shows no availability degradation above tolerance AND no automatic rollback). Baseline success = 1,196/1,199 (0.9974979149); guarded success = 1,199/1,199 (1.0000000000). Paired‑success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0025020851 (95% bootstrap percentile CI [0.0000, 0.0058381985], bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10,000); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25. Provider audit shows model_calls_used = 1,203 and repair calls = 3. Given the preregistered minimum detectable effect of 5 percentage points and the observed near‑ceiling baseline, the study was underpowered to detect the observed ≈0.25 pp absolute gain. Under the chosen synthetic corpus and validator settings, the verifier rarely intervened; we archive full artifacts, analysis code, and seeds to enable sensitivity studies that vary task ambiguity, verifier strictness, and model families.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are being proposed to translate operator intent expressed in natural language into executable device configurations for network operations (NetOps). Surveys and system work emphasize that operational reliability depends on orchestration, deterministic validators, and assurance infrastructure rather than on the base LLM alone. A common mitigation pattern is a generate–validate–repair (verifier‑assisted) architecture: the LLM proposes a candidate configuration, an automated verifier checks constraints and safety, and an automated repair loop iterates until verifier rules are satisfied. Despite this conceptual support, publicly archived, preregistered paired evidence measuring whether verifier assistance yields an operationally meaningful improvement (rollback‑aware binary success) relative to one‑shot generation is limited.

We address this gap with NetOpsTraceBench (preregistration ID rX4f7-1). The central research question is: Can a reproducible, workflow‑centered benchmark of paired intent→config episodes produce an objective paired binary success metric that reliably distinguishes verifier‑assisted pipelines from one‑shot generation across two simulated topology clusters? Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered experimental design and frozen analysis plan (preregistration SHA‑256 = 77abe8b4...5712) executed end‑to‑end under deterministic components; (2) a complete paired analysis on 1,199 completed pairs using requested_model = gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 with explicit reporting of analytic deviation (Wilcoxon planned → exact McNemar executed for binary outcomes); and (3) comprehensive archival artifacts (model outputs, validator traces, provider audit, analysis code and seeds) that quantify why repair was rarely needed and that enable follow‑up sensitivity experiments.
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and system papers position LLMs within AIOps/NetOps pipelines and emphasize the importance of verifiers, provenance, and workflow‑centered evaluation. Prior work on verifier‑guided NL→formal translations and intent→topology compilation demonstrates feasibility of generate–validate‑repair approaches for formal artifacts and security topologies, while other prototypes show LLMs can produce device configurations and catch misconfigurations on constructed corpora. Empirical and conceptual studies document LLM failure modes relevant to NetOps—hallucination, incorrect semantics/units, overconfidence, provenance loss, and prompt injection—which motivate guarded architectures and runtime auditing. Those surveys call for benchmarks that measure trace quality, rollback behavior, and canary‑style checks instead of one‑shot QA metrics; NetOpsTraceBench operationalizes a paired, rollback‑aware binary success metric in a preregistered framework and supplies run artifacts to enable reproducible interpretation.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and scope: We froze the study design before execution (rX4f7-1; preregistration SHA‑256 = 77abe8b4...5712). NetOpsTraceBench_v1 comprises 1,200 paired intent→config tasks split into two topology clusters (edge=600, core=600). Tasks are public synthetic or consented with deterministic provenance tags. Inclusion/exclusion rules were deterministic: pairs were excluded if contamination detection flagged potential training‑data overlap above preregistered thresholds or if both episodes failed to produce parsable vendor renderings after a single automated re‑execution attempt; exclusions are logged. The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline using the preregistered complete_pair_primary treatment.

Pipelines and instrumentation: We compared (A) Baseline one‑shot — a single LLM call producing an initial candidate configuration; and (B) Guarded verifier‑assisted — the same shared initial candidate plus at most one automated repair iteration when the deterministic validator rejected the candidate. Orchestration used adapter hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and the requested model was gpt-5-mini (provider recorded as openai_responses). Deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performed parsing, intent‑constraint validation, and emulator preflight checks; deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 produced tasks. Model configuration recorded requested_model=gpt-5-mini and max_output_tokens=1500; execution manifest reports model_calls_used = 1,203 and maximum_model_calls = 2,400.

Success rule, preregistered analysis, and analytic deviation: The preregistered binary episode success rule required (1) validator acceptance of the final configuration, (2) emulator execution without availability degradation exceeding the preregistered tolerance, and (3) no automatic rollback during simulated execution. The preregistration specified a nonparametric paired procedure (Wilcoxon signed‑rank) for paired outcomes; because realized outcomes are strictly binary, the archived confirmatory analysis used an exact McNemar two‑sided test on the 2×2 contingency table and computed a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the paired success‑rate difference (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000). This post‑preregistration analytic choice and all analysis code and seeds are archived (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). The preregistered power plan targeted an absolute MDE of 5 percentage points at two‑sided α=0.05 and power=0.8 given assumed baseline ≈0.70; that MDE informs interpretation of the observed results (see Results and Discussion).
sections.results:
Execution accounting and artifacts: Planned episodes = 2,400 (1,200 pairs); completed_episode_count = 2,398; failed_episode_count = 2; complete_pair_count = 1,199. Provider audit: hosted_model_call_event_count = 1,203; completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 1,202; failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 1. Stage counts show shared_initial_generation = 1,200 and repair = 3, i.e., the guarded pipeline triggered repair calls only three times. Artifact_count for the run = 8,408; representative validator traces and scoring artifacts are archived (examples include execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json).

Primary confirmatory outcomes (archived analysis): complete_pair_count = 1,199; baseline_success_count = 1,196 (baseline_success_rate = 0.9974979149291076); guarded_success_count = 1,199 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). Paired contingency counts: n11 = 1,196; n10 = 3 (guarded success only); n01 = 0; n00 = 0 (see analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). Paired‑success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002502085070892446. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples) = [0.0000, 0.005838198498748957]. Missingness: failed_baseline_episodes = 1; failed_guarded_episodes = 1; both_missing_pairs = 1 (see analysis/missingness_summary.csv).

Representative validator diagnostics: Scoring artifacts show that for typical tasks the initial shared candidate satisfied intent constraints and validator checks (e.g., execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json reports validation_after.valid = true and repair_applied = false). The low repair invocation count (3) is corroborated by provider audit stage_counts. Together these artifacts indicate that, under the chosen validator configuration and synthetic task corpus, LLM initial candidates were accepted in the vast majority of episodes, leaving little operational headroom for guard‑triggered improvement.
sections.discussion:
Statistical interpretation and power: The exact McNemar test and bootstrap CI indicate no statistically significant advantage for the guarded pipeline in this run (p = 0.25; 95% CI includes zero). Crucially, the preregistered power plan targeted an MDE of 5 percentage points (absolute) at α=0.05 and power=0.8 under an assumed baseline ≈0.70. The observed baseline ≈0.9975 dramatically reduced available absolute headroom; detecting the observed ≈0.25 percentage‑point improvement would require many more discordant pairs or a task corpus with substantially lower baseline success. The archived contingency counts (n10=3, n01=0) and CI quantify this limited power and justify cautious interpretation: a null result here does not imply verifiers are unhelpful in general.

Operational root causes supported by artifacts: Two artifact‑grounded explanations account for the small measured gain. First, the synthetic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) produced tasks with explicit required sequences and constrained intents; representative task_manifest entries show required_sequence fields and conservative constraints that reduce ambiguity. Second, the deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and its acceptance thresholds were configured so that many initial candidates passed intent‑constraint checks without repair. The provider audit (repair stage = 3) and scoring traces jointly support that corpus design and validator strictness materially reduced repair invocation frequency.

Threats to validity and externality: Internal validity is high for deterministic components (frozen seeds, deterministic task generation, automated exclusion rules) and analytic reproducibility (archived analysis code and seeds). Construct validity depends on whether the binary success rule (validator acceptance + emulator availability tolerance + no rollback) maps to production operational correctness; this mapping is an open question. External validity is limited by (1) single requested model family (gpt-5-mini), (2) synthetic/consented task corpus with vendor‑agnostic canonical renderings, and (3) Mininet‑style emulation that may not capture vendor idiosyncrasies or complex routing convergence. Conclusion validity is constrained by low discordant counts and the preregistered MDE; practitioners should not generalize this null finding to different corpora, verifiers, or model families.

Practical implications and recommended follow‑ups: When initial generation already meets deterministic verifier criteria for well‑specified tasks, generate–validate–repair will be infrequently exercised and measured gains on a binary success metric will be small. To evaluate verifier value more incisively, future benchmarks should (a) introduce controlled ambiguity and adversarial perturbations to task intents, (b) vary verifier strictness and parsing sensitivity, (c) exercise multiple LLM families and fine‑tuned variants, and (d) measure graded outcome metrics (e.g., severity‑weighted violations, repair iterations, time‑to‑repair) in addition to binary success. The archived artifacts and traces permit exact reproduction and targeted sensitivity analyses along these axes.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed NetOpsTraceBench, a paired, emulator‑grounded study comparing one‑shot and verifier‑assisted NL→configuration pipelines on 1,199 completed pairs. Under our synthetic task corpus, deterministic validator settings, and requested_model = gpt-5-mini, baseline one‑shot generation achieved near‑ceiling success (≈99.75%). The guarded pipeline increased absolute success by ≈0.25 percentage points (paired difference = 0.0025020851) with exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25 and a 95% bootstrap CI that includes zero. Archived execution manifests, provider audits (model_calls_used = 1,203; repairs invoked = 3), validator traces, and analysis artifacts support the interpretation that the observed null result reflects limited headroom given task and validator choices, not definitive evidence that verifiers are never useful. We release full artifacts and seeds to enable reproducible sensitivity studies that vary task ambiguity, verifier strictness, and model families to identify conditions where verifier scaffolding yields operationally meaningful improvements.

limitations: Single model family tested (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across other LLMs or fine‑tuned variants.

Task corpus skew: synthetic/consented tasks yielded near‑ceiling baseline success (≈99.75%), limiting headroom and statistical power to detect practical improvements by guarded pipelines — the preregistered MDE was 5 percentage points (α=0.05, power=0.8), so the observed ≈0.25 pp effect lies well below the planned MDE.

Emulator fidelity: Mininet‑style emulation and deterministic validators approximate production behavior but may not capture all deployment failure modes (routing convergence, vendor idiosyncrasies, transient telemetry).

Verifier configuration dependence: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 acceptance thresholds and parsing rules materially affect outcomes; different verifier strictness could change repair invocation rates and measured gains.

Synthetic task design likely reduced baseline difficulty: representative task_manifest entries include explicit required_sequence constraints and conservative intent specifications (e.g., task-000001 required_sequence), which, together with the validator configuration, explain the low repair invocation count (repair = 3) observed in provider audit.

Analytic deviation documented: the preregistration specified a Wilcoxon signed‑rank paired procedure; because outcomes were binary the archived confirmatory analysis used an exact McNemar test. This deviation and its artifacts are recorded and archived.
Operational external validity: absence of heterogeneous vendor renderers, real production templates, and live rollouts constrain direct production generalization.
